{"self_assessment": "Impact
I proposed the fish at the very start and drew it on the pad. The outline reads clearly with a big rounded body and a forked tail. I laid the start domino and the first stroke, the top of the body from the nose, which everything else grows from. As a result about 130 of the 145 standing dominoes were connected to the start when the push came, and the body and both tails were lit.

Execution
I sketched the fish with curves rather than corners so one push could run through it, and I numbered the strokes so each person had a clear piece. I closed the gap near the nose so the top curve connected. When the lower tail wouldn't catch at the crossing, I relaid it from scratch and it lit up. I also inspected the crossing, tails and loop several times to see what would actually fall. I worked on the tail loop on the right until late, and it did not light up in the end.

Collaboration
I gave Sofia, Omar and Jack each a stroke and told them to start once the lines reached them. I asked people to keep clear of the spots I was working on, so we didn't bump each other. I took Sofia's offer to fix the notch from the top while I worked from below. In the last two minutes I asked everyone to go hands-off so nothing got bumped before the push.

Leadership
I set the plan in the first seconds: the animal, the sketch and who did which stroke. I kept the table coordinated and kept updating everyone on what I was doing. I made the call to stop working on the loop and protect the lit body and tails, and kept everyone's hands off for the final stretch.", "my_share_percent": 40}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took ownership of the upper tail (stroke 3) and laid it from the crossing through to the loop at the right end, so the fish has a clear, readable tail and the judge gets a complete fish silhouette. Execution: I started the upper tail early, laying it in steady batches from about 1:30 onward, then inspected the area twice to check it. When the chain needed extending near the loop I carried the line on with several more batches, and I confirmed the upper tail was fully in and lit before the final minutes. I then went hands-off so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I kept the table updated on where the upper tail stood, so Hana and the others always knew its status. I kept away from other people's work areas, particularly the crossing and the bottom-right corner, to avoid bumping. I backed the plan to stay hands-off at the end.

Leadership: I helped keep the mood upbeat and the team energised. I flagged the time checks and reminded everyone to keep fingers off before the push. I committed to the fish plan quickly, which let the tail strokes get started in parallel and kept the build moving.

Overall, the upper tail was a key part of making the fish read as a fish, and I delivered it reliably and on time. I'd put my share of the result at around 30 percent.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I took ownership of the lower tail (stroke 4) at the start and traced it from the crossing outward over several passes, standing dominoes back up where needed. Execution: I picked one stroke and stuck with it, working steadily without pulling others off their own pieces. Collaboration: I stayed clear of the corner Hana and Sofia were working on, so we didn't knock each other's work over. I backed Sofia's and Hana's fixes rather than competing with them.

Leadership: I led by example on discipline. I committed to a stroke early, called out my status clearly, and joined the hands-off call before the push to protect the lit fish. I supported Hana's plan and kept the table's communication calm and positive in the last minutes.

Overall, I delivered my assigned piece of a fish that reads clearly as a fish, and I helped keep the table stable through the final stretch.", "my_share_percent": 22}
